question.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Not a Polynomial
question.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=-\frac{4}{(2+t)^{2}}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s}$, find the velocity (in $\text{m}/\text{s}$) of the particle at time $t.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-\frac{4}{(2+t)^{2}})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{2+t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{4}{2+0}+C \\ 2 & =2+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{4}{2+t}.$

evidence.solution_quote: Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{4}{2+t}.$
